title: Not All Dissents Are Created Equal
hook: Dissent tallies treat a one-line 'I would deny' the same as a fully reasoned opinion. One scholar sorted 386 of them on the emergency docket — and found about half were just bare votes.
key_points: Davis sorts emergency-docket dissents into four kinds — from full authored opinions down to bare 'would grant/deny' votes.
Of 386 objections she counted, about half were bare notations with no reasoning — yet standard tallies count them like full opinions.
Per-justice gaps are large: Sotomayor logged 65 objections but 15 authored opinions; Thomas 57 objections, only 3 authored.
Justices write more when the stakes suit them: 78% of 'judicial power' cases drew written dissents, versus 27% of criminal-procedure cases.
The 2024–25 term saw 23 authored dissents — the most in 25 years — as executive-order challenges crowded the emergency docket.
content_html: We often measure how divided the Supreme Court is by counting dissents. But a dissent can be a fully reasoned opinion — or just a one-line note that a justice "would have denied" the request. Political scientist Taraleigh Davis argues that lumping the two together makes the Court's fast-moving emergency docket look far more reasoned than it actually is.
extra_html: Writing for SCOTUSblog, Davis — a public-law scholar at Bradley University — sorts emergency-docket objections into four tiers: authored opinions that explain the disagreement, opinions a justice merely joins, "noted" dissents that record disagreement without explanation, and bare "would grant/deny" notations that state only a vote. Of the 386 objections she catalogued, roughly half were that last, bare kind — yet conventional counts treat them the same as full opinions. The per-justice picture varies sharply: Justice Sotomayor recorded 65 objections but only 15 authored opinions, while Justice Thomas had 57 objections with just 3 authored and 41 bare notations; Justice Jackson stood out for writing 11 authored dissents in only three terms. Justices also seem to reserve their reasoning for the cases they care about most — about 78% of cases touching "judicial power" drew a written dissent, against only 27% of criminal-procedure cases. And the volume is climbing: the 2024–25 term produced 23 authored dissents, the most in a quarter-century, as emergency challenges to executive orders multiplied. The civics takeaway is a caution about metrics: a raw dissent count can overstate how much explanation actually accompanies the Court's fastest, least-transparent decisions. (This card describes U.S. Supreme Court practice specifically.)

related.title: The Supreme Court's 'Shadow Docket'
related.hook: Most Supreme Court rulings today aren't fully-argued opinions — they're fast, often unsigned orders with little explanation. In the term ending October 2025, those quietly became the majority.

related.title: The Power of a Dissent
related.hook: A dissenting judge loses the case — but a sharp dissent can outlive the majority, persuading future courts or pushing lawmakers to rewrite the rule.

related.title: How the Supreme Court Decides a Case
related.hook: A top court hears only a sliver of the cases that beg for its attention — and the path from petition to ruling runs through written briefs, a public argument, and a vote taken in secret.

related.title: Nine Justices, Nine Styles
related.hook: One scholar coded 5,095 questions from a full Supreme Court term and found each justice interrogates lawyers in a signature way — a fingerprint of how they think about the law.
